practice1.prompt: Open notes.txt in write mode, write Hello, World! into it, close it, then print File created and closed successfully

cases.name: says the file was created and closed
the file is closed, not just opened
cases.describe: close() called on the file that open() returned

practice1.hint: The lesson's pattern is open, use, close. The message at the end is only true once all three have happened.

questions.prompt: What does open("notes.txt", "w") do to a file that already exists?
choices: Adds to the end of it
Leaves it alone until you write
questions.explain: Write mode truncates. If the old contents matter, append mode is the one you want.

questions.prompt: What happens with open("missing.txt", "r") when the file is not there?
choices: It waits for the file to appear
questions.explain: Read mode never creates anything. The file has to exist, and if it does not you get FileNotFoundError.

questions.prompt: Match each mode to what it does.
right: Adds to the end, keeping what was there
questions.explain: The three modes differ in what they do to the existing contents: read touches nothing, write throws it away, append keeps it and adds.
open() hands back a file object and close() releases it. Until close runs, what you wrote may still be sitting in a buffer rather than on disk.

questions.prompt: Why does forgetting close() matter, even though the program still ends?
choices: What you wrote may never reach the disk, and the file stays locked while the program runs
Python refuses to open any more files
It does not matter at all
questions.explain: Writes are buffered. Closing is what flushes them and hands the file back to the operating system.

reflection-exercise1.hint: Say what each mode does to the text that was already in the file, then name a job that wants each behaviour.

reflection-exercise2.hint: Think about where your text actually is between the write() call and the close() call.
